Retired Air Force lieutenant colonel and federal agent. She hunted terror networks, spies and child predators. Now she's Montana's Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, and she can't be bought.
Your ballot is in the mail. Mail it back or drop it off at your county election office. It has to arrive by 8 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
## She shows her work. Check it.
Four candidates are on your ballot. These are the differences, and every claim links to the proof.
On the record on 136 of 140 issues
Your voter guide puts all four candidates side by side on 140 questions, with every answer sourced to their own words. Alani has a stated position on almost every one. The others leave dozens blank.

She can't be bought
Zero corporate PAC money. She backs I-194, The Montana Plan, to end dark money in Montana.
She's done the job
21 years in the Air Force and a career as a federal agent. She led a counterintelligence task force that caught spies, directed more than 180 agents across eight countries, and built coalitions of federal, state, local and nonprofit organizations to go after child predators.
She answers the questions
Her answers to voter questionnaires are published, side by side with her opponents', so you can compare for yourself.
Montana chose her
Montana Democrats chose her in an open primary. She'll serve as a Democrat; the independent says he'll caucus with neither party.

Every attack tracked this campaign, answered with the record and the sources.

pages.text:
Service Record · Alani Bankhead for U.S. Senate in Montana
## Alani I. Bankhead
Lieutenant Colonel, U.S. Air Force (Retired)
Twenty-one years of service, in and out of uniform. Her records are below.
A career in brief. Hover a year to see the role, or tap it to jump to that part of her record.
Lieutenant Colonel Alani Bankhead retired from the United States Air Force on 1 October 2025 after more than 21 years of commissioned service, transferring to the Retired Reserve effective 26 February 2026. She served as a supervisory special agent with the Air Force Office of Special Investigations, the Air Force's federal law enforcement and counterintelligence organization.
2004 to 2013
Commissioned through Air Force ROTC, May 2004, with her sister.
She was commissioned in May 2004 through Air Force ROTC at The Pennsylvania State University and entered active duty that July. Her early career was in personnel and readiness at Lajes Field in the Azores, followed by section command at Tinker Air Force Base.
In 2008 and 2009 she cross-trained into Special Investigations, completing the Criminal Investigator Training Program and the Basic Special Investigators Course, and served as an OSI operations officer at Misawa Air Base, Japan, where she was one of the Air Force's first agents trained for Internet Crimes Against Children task force work. While at Misawa, she deployed with Special Operations to neutralize Al Qaeda leaders.
She then served as Chief of AFOSI Research, Development and Acquisition in Quantico, Virginia, leading the counter-intelligence mission that kept spies and terrorists from getting access to our most classified research and technologies.
2013 to 2016
Pentagon security detail.
She then commanded an OSI detachment in Kuwait, and later served as the senior bodyguard and Security Advisor to the Secretary of the Air Force.
Special agents spend much of their careers out of uniform.
Deployed commanders take a turn serving the holiday meal. It is a small, standing tradition, but it's the small gestures that matter, and Alani always shows up for her people.
On the serving line at the deployed holiday meal.
The same holiday meal.
2016 to 2026
Upon entering the Reserves, Alani also began her civilian career. These civilian positions are captured separately from her military service record, and are detailed further down on the page.
Presenting a promotion certificate.
In 2016 she moved from active duty to the Air Force Reserve as an Individual Mobilization Augmentee (IMA), filling specialized roles inside active-duty units and major commands. She served as the IMA to the Commander of MacDill Air Force Base, Florida, responsible for providing investigative and counter-intelligence services to SOCOM and CENTCOM.
In 2022 she moved to AFOSI Headquarters in Quantico, Virginia, as the IMA to the Assistant Director and Special Agent in Charge, overseeing 60 investigators drawn from seventeen law enforcement agencies working child exploitation cases.
Her career closed as the IMA to the Commander of the 7th Field Investigations Squadron at Joint Base Andrews, the Office of Special Investigations' National Capital Region command, which supports Headquarters Air Force, the Space Force, the Joint Staff and the Office of the Secretary of Defense.
At the Office of Special Investigations 2025 conference, in her last year in uniform.
Awards and decorations
During her service, Lt Col Bankhead accumulated four years and five months of foreign service. She earned an Iraq Campaign Medal with service star, 5 Meritorious Service Medals, 2 Air and Space Commendation Medals, Joint Service Achievement Medal, 3 Air and Space Achievement Medals, Meritorious Unit Award, Air and Space Organizational Excellence Award, National Defense Service Medal, Global War On Terrorism Expeditionary Medal, Global War on Terrorism Service Medal, 2 Air and Space Overseas Service Ribbons Short, Air and Space Overseas Service Ribbon Long, 5 Air and Space Longevity Service Awards, 2 Small Arms Expert Marksmanship Ribbons, and Air and Space Training Ribbon. She also completed Air War College.
Education and training
B.A., Latin American Studies and Criminal Justice, minor in Military Studies
The Pennsylvania State University
Aerospace Basic Course
Criminal Investigator Training Program
Federal Law Enforcement Training Center
Basic Special Investigators Course
U.S. Air Force Special Investigations Academy
Squadron Officer School
M.S., International Relations, concentration in International Security Studies
Air Command and Staff College
Air War College
Effective dates of promotion
Second Lieutenant, 16 June 2004
First Lieutenant, 16 June 2006
Captain, 16 June 2008
Major, 1 December 2014
Lieutenant Colonel, 1 December 2021
These are Lt Col Bankhead's DD-214s, released by her. Personal identifiers such as Social Security number, date of birth, and home address are covered. Nothing about her service, rank, assignments, or decorations is withheld.
A DD-214 is a federal form, built as a government record predominantly for service benefits rather than for public consumption. This means that they aren't always the easiest to read. Someone who serves only on active duty gets one when they leave, covering that whole period. A reservist's records are not handled the same way: each deployment or mobilization is a separate period of service, and each one ends with its own DD-214. Each is accurate, but each shows only its own slice. That is why we've included two forms here. The first is from when she transitioned from active duty to the Reserve, and the second is from when she retired.
Active duty, 2004 to 2016
Block 12 shows 11 years, 5 months and 14 days of net active service and 4 years, 5 months and 16 days of foreign service. Block 24 records the character of service as honorable.
This form totals the career: 13 years and 5 months of active service and 7 years, 10 months of inactive service. It closes out on 30 September 2025; her retirement was effective the following day. It runs to a second page, which opens with the first.
Select either form to open it full size.
We're also including a couple of her decoration citations, written and signed by the commander who approved the award, as well as a letter of appreciation from a partner police agency overseas.
Meritorious Service Medal, first oak leaf cluster
30 May 2022 to 31 May 2024. Signed by Brigadier General Amy S. Bumgarner, Commander of the Air Force Office of Special Investigations.
Colonel Bankhead masterfully oversaw 60 investigators from seventeen multi-jurisdictional law enforcement agencies working child exploitation allegations, achieving a multitude of arrests followed by an unparalleled prosecution rate.
Her professionalism and leadership during one of the most extensive proactive operations against child sex abuse in the DoD was key to training agents, prosecutors, and intelligence analysts from various departments, resulting in 120 arrests and a 96 percent conviction rate.
Finally, Colonel Bankhead's analysis of warfighting operations and lessons learned enhanced the command's capacity to develop three critical policy processes supporting agents deployed for counterintelligence and counter-terrorism missions, ultimately protecting the Department of the Air Force from threats.
Air Force Commendation Medal, first oak leaf cluster
16 March 2009 to 30 June 2011. Signed by Colonel Sarah L. Garcia, Commander of the 6th Field Investigations Region. Covers her time as an operations officer at Misawa Air Base, Japan.
Agent Robles's outstanding initiative as one of the Air Force's first Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force trained agents resulted in the primary coordination in Japan with Federal Bureau of Investigation's Legal Attaché and United States Immigrations and Customs Enforcement that led to successful proactive operations at Air Force Office of Special Investigations units across the Pacific Region.
The citation is in her former name. She served under Robles until 2016, which is also the name on her active duty DD-214.
Select either citation to open it full size.
Japanese National Police, Aomori Prefecture
26 October 2011. Signed and sealed by Shigeki Sasaki, Police Superintendent, Chief of Misawa Police Station.
You have positively cooperated with the Japanese police, which resulted in the apprehension of a suspect who violated the Law on Punishing Acts related to Child Prostitution and Child Pornography, and for protecting Children that occurred in the Aomori prefecture.
Upon entering the Reserves, Alani also began her civilian career. These civilian positions are captured separately from her military service record.
From September 2016 to November 2017 she was International Director of Investigations and Law Enforcement Development for Latin America at the International Justice Mission (IJM), the world's largest anti-slavery organization—a nonprofit whose teams investigate slavery, child sexual assault and the commercial sexual exploitation of children, and work with host nation governments to prosecute offenders and support survivors. Her work there focused on child sexual abuse and child sex trafficking.
In April 2018 she joined the State of Hawaii Department of the Attorney General as a special agent in its Internet Crimes Against Children unit, later serving as alternate commander, through December 2021. She took the task force training she had done in the Air Force and put it to work standing up Hawaii's ICAC operation, which had been struggling to recruit and hold investigators. She was also the unit's electronic detection K9 handler, working with a dog trained to find concealed digital storage devices during search warrants.
The Hawaii ICAC Task Force ran the first Operation Keiki Shield on Oahu in March 2019—an operation to identify, locate and arrest offenders who commit internet-facilitated sexual crimes against children, and to identify and rescue child victims of child sexual exploitation and abuse. In the Attorney General's announcement that November, the operations had involved 95 law enforcement officers and professional staff from more than a dozen county, state, federal and military agencies, and produced 25 arrests across the first three operations. Alani continued to run these operations until her departure in December 2021. The recognition below covers Keiki Shield I through XI, March 2019 to December 2021. The program is still running: its twenty-ninth operation was announced in November 2025.
During this time she also created Operation Shine the Light with the Attorney General's Missing Child Center, a recurring, multi-agency initiative on Oʻahu aimed at locating and recovering endangered missing children and runaways who are at high risk of exploitation, abuse, and human trafficking. The first operation ran in October 2020 and recovered five children from the foster care system. Since then the initiative has recovered 64 children across the island.
Hawaii Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force
March 2019 to December 2021. Presented by the State of Hawaii Department of the Attorney General on behalf of the NCIS Hawaii Field Office, for Operation Keiki Shield I through XI.
Mighty Sparrow Coaching
Alongside that work, Alani founded Mighty Sparrow Coaching, a service-disabled veteran-owned small business, and became a certified professional coach through the International Coaching Federation. A large part of the business is training: she teaches law enforcement officers, prosecutors, and judges, in the United States and abroad, how to better protect children and women from sexual abuse, assault, exploitation, and trafficking. That means the practical side of the work, like combining investigative work with intelligence to find offenders and the children they harm, and building cases that end in convictions. As she puts it, if she can teach others to do this work, “now we’re force multiplying.”
The rest of her practice is one-on-one and group coaching. Many of her clients are accomplished women who, despite real success, live with what’s called imposter syndrome: a persistent feeling that they haven’t really earned where they are, and that sooner or later someone will find out. “The biggest imposter statements we see are ‘I am not smart enough’ and ‘I don’t have the credentials,’” she has said. Her coaching starts from a simple idea: “the thing that you think is your greatest weakness is actually the key to unlocking your greatest power.”
That same fear of not being enough often shows up in how people handle money, so the coaching grew to include money habits. Some of her clients earn a good living and still feel like they never have enough: they overspend, avoid looking at their finances, or can’t save no matter what they make. She calls the work moving from a scarcity mindset to an abundance mindset, which means learning to manage what you already have instead of chasing more. It is coaching on habits and mindset, not investment, tax, or legal advice.
A letter of recommendation
Kevin K. Takata spent thirty-three years as a prosecutor in Hawaii, including as chief of the Criminal Justice Division in the Hawaii Attorney General's office. He hired Alani into the state's Internet Crimes Against Children unit in 2018. He wrote this in March 2023, and it is published here with his permission.
March 29, 2023
Letter of Recommendation
Re: Alani Bankhead, Special Agent Par Excellence
During my thirty-three year career as a prosecutor in Hawaii, I worked with a multitude of federal, state and local law enforcement personnel who ranged from the leaders of their agencies or departments, to seasoned investigators, to recently hired officers, in my roles as a member of a homicide team (I'm credited with the most homicide convictions in Hawaii), chief of the felony trials division in the Honolulu prosecutors' office, first deputy in the Kauai prosecutors' office, and chief of the Criminal Justice Division in the Hawaii Attorney General's office. One person distinguished herself from the rest with her relentless pursuit of those who preyed on children, passion to serve her community and country, and ability to organize and execute undercover operations. That person is Alani Bankhead.
We first met in 2018 to discuss her interest in a special agent position with the Internet Crimes Against Children (“ICAC”) unit. At that time, ICAC was performing poorly and was having difficulty recruiting and retaining investigators, in part due to having to deal with the horrendous child pornography images possessed and distributed by suspects. Ms. Bankhead impressed me with her desire to handle these difficult investigations, and more.
I hired her and it turned out to be one of the best decisions I made during my career. Ms. Bankhead revitalized the ICAC unit. She was the heart and soul behind a still ongoing series of undercover operations that involved law enforcement officers posing as adolescents online to entice pedophiles to make contact and meet. She arranged to train the officers, and planned, participated in and helped supervise the operations.
Training, organizing and supervising undercover operations involving federal, state and local law enforcement personnel with the attendant egos is never easy, but Ms. Bankhead was able to get the different personalities and agencies to work together. Everything from officer safety, logistics (e.g., securing a house to meet the suspects at, setting up a command center, food for the participants, evidence collection, etc.), and legal issues were addressed. It is a testament to Ms. Bankhead's leadership that most of suspects who were arrested pled guilty even while facing lengthy prison terms.
The undercover operations were expanded from Honolulu to other Hawaiian islands (Hawaii island, Kauai and Maui) and Guam, where it met with equal success. During the operations, child sex abuse and human trafficking victims were identified and rescued. The Hawaii Legislature must have been impressed because for the first time Hawaii's ICAC unit received state funding and didn't have to rely exclusively on federal dollars.
If that wasn't enough, Ms. Bankhead secured an electronic detection dog for Hawaii (aka “Lulu”) who is trained to sniff out digital storage devices that are used to store child pornography. Lulu and Ms. Bankhead were an inseparable team that were called upon for search warrant executions and prison searches. Lulu soon became a celebrity for her work and has been honored from Honolulu to Washington, D.C.
Ms. Bankhead is dedicated to protecting the vulnerable, investigating criminal activity and thereby preserving the rule of law. She has a proven ability to work with people of disparate backgrounds for a common good. And, most importantly, she is passionate in all she does.
It was my good fortune that our paths crossed for she was instrumental in improving the Hawaii ICAC unit and the lives of children in Hawaii.
Kevin K. Takata
The letter as written.
A colleague on the work
Kaleilani Grant is Assistant Coordinator of the Missing Child Center Hawaii at the Hawaii Department of the Attorney General, where she has served since 2018. She is a Native Hawaiian survivor of sex trafficking, a recipient of the U.S. Department of Justice Child Protection Award, and attended the 2023 State of the Union as the guest of U.S. Senator Mazie Hirono. She and Alani worked in neighbouring units at the Attorney General's office.
Alani and I met in 2018 in Honolulu, Hawaii, where we both worked for the Department of the Attorney General's office. There I served in a unit called the Missing Child Center, where I recovered missing and exploited children, and Alani served in a unit called ICAC, or the Internet Crimes Against Children. There we decided to partner together, our teams united, to really not only identify what the issue was with missing and exploited children but identify the bad guys. And Alani, from the get-go, was very passionate, very driven.
Through that partnership we were able to come up with the very first operation for the state of Hawaii, and that was an operation dedicated to not only identify the perpetrators and the missing children but recover those children who were missing, who were being exploited, who were being abused.
And because of that, Alani not only built a legacy that continues on till this day, but she impacted so many lives, she saved so many lives. She is very intentional, she's very strategic on her efforts, and Alani is one that will not just talk the talk but she will walk it out. She will do what she says. She's committed, she dedicates everything within her to do what she says she's going to do, and that is one thing that I admire about Alani: that she is a woman of her word, she is a woman of integrity, she's honest, she's transparent, there's no hidden agenda.
And for one who has worked with the government closely, has worked with politicians, has worked with law enforcement, has worked with victims, survivors, their families, I've worked in this arena for over 16 years now, and there is no one, it is undeniable that Alani is the one person that I would trust completely. If my child went missing, there was something going on in my community, if there was one representative that I would want speaking on my behalf, that would be Alani.
Kaleilani Grant, July 2026. Watch on YouTube.

- Hawaii Department of the Attorney General, News Release 2021-36 (25 May 2021). The U.S. Department of Justice Child Protection Award to the Missing Child Center Hawaii. Records the first Operation Shine the Light in October 2020 as a partnership between the Center and the Hawaii ICAC Task Force, and names Alani Bankhead, then an ICAC Task Force special agent, as the person who submitted the winning nomination.

- Penn State Department of Sociology and Criminology, Outstanding Alumni Award, 2024, which recognizes her training of justice system professionals.
- Georgetown Security Studies Review, Precision-Guided Podcast, Ep. 55 (January 2024), “Imposter Syndrome with Alani Bankhead,” on her work as a coach and consultant to U.S. and international law enforcement, prosecutors, victim services, and judicial professionals.

Twenty-one years of service.
Where she stands now is on the issues page.

pages.title: Rumors About Alani Bankhead, Answered · Alani Bankhead for Senate
pages.text:
Rumors About Alani Bankhead, Answered · Alani Bankhead for Senate
## Heard something about Alani? Here’s the record.
Mailers, TV ads and a lot of rumors. Here are the 61 claims we’ve tracked against her this campaign, each one answered with the record behind it.
## Got a dirty-money mailer or saw one of their TV ads?
Seth Bodnar’s campaign and the super PACs backing him have flooded Montana with mailers and commercials about Alani. We put every one of them side by side with the facts.
- The church, the publisher and the “dark money” attacks
- The Planned Parenthood mailers
- The spliced quotes and the TV ads
## The rumors about her service
Most of what’s on this page started as a post, a screenshot or a secondhand comment on social media, then got passed along until it sounded like fact. It’s a game of telephone, and not one of these claims came with a document behind it. Some have gone as far as disrespectful claims of stolen valor against a highly decorated military retiree.
Alani’s full history of service has been posted online for anyone to see at alaniformt.com/service. So let’s take the rumors you may have heard, one at a time.
Ask yourself why. It’s easy for people to believe a white male candidate was a Green Beret, with no scrutiny, no proof, and no questions about his mission or how long he held that role. Seth Bodnar has released one DD-214, from when he left active duty in 2011. [1] Since then he served in the Army Reserve, which has no Green Berets, and then in a Montana National Guard headquarters assignment that the Guard itself called “not a highly deployable asset.” [2][3] Almost no one has asked what his military role has been since. His service is honorable, and that isn’t the point. The point is the double standard: when a strong woman of color runs for office, suddenly she couldn’t possibly have had an impressive military and law-enforcement career.
Alani has published her service record in full: both DD-214s, her decoration citations, and letters from the people she worked alongside. [4][5][6] When Sen. Tammy Duckworth’s war record came under attack in her 2016 race, she released years of her own medical records, with a doctor’s letter declaring her fit to serve. [7]
Her military record is “unverifiable.” It’s just her word.
Her DD-214s and decoration citations are posted in full at alaniformt.com/service. [4][5] A DD-214 is issued by the military, not the service member. [8] Each citation carries an order number and the signature of the awarding officer, and her Meritorious Service Medal was signed by the general who now commands the entire Air Force Office of Special Investigations. [5][9]
Other veterans’ DD-214s count. Hers doesn’t.
A DD-214 is the military’s own record of service, whoever it belongs to. [8] Alani has posted both of hers, plus her citations. [4][5] It’s the same document every veteran relies on, and it deserves the same standard.
If she had nothing to hide, she’d just sign a FOIA request.
A public records request returns a short list of basics: dates of service, rank, assignments, and which awards someone was eligible for. It doesn’t return the citations, evaluations or orders. [10] Alani has already published more than a records request would ever produce. [4][5]
“I know people who were at the same base,” and they say she exaggerates.
Sharing a base tells you nothing about someone else’s job. Soldiers in a different service and an unrelated unit have no window into a compartmented Air Force counterintelligence officer’s work. And no one has ever said what, specifically, they contradicted.
“Squadron commander in Iraq” is a story she made up.
She commanded an Air Force Office of Special Investigations unit in the Gulf and served in Iraq, and she described that work in a 2020 interview, years before she ran. [11][12] Her Iraq Campaign Medal and Global War on Terrorism Expeditionary Medal are on her DD-214. [4]
“Shot at and mortared” is overblown.
Alani served in Iraq running intelligence operations against Al-Qaeda, and she described that work on the record in 2020, long before the campaign. [12] Her Iraq Campaign Medal is on her DD-214. [4]
She claims a connection to Black Hawk Down.
She never has. What is on the record: a retired Army Ranger and author, Jeff Struecker, said on his own podcast in 2024 that part of one of his novels was based on Iraq work she did, and that he knows “firsthand of the lives that you saved.” [13] Her Iraq service is on her DD-214. [4]
Her “96 percent conviction rate” can’t be found anywhere.
It’s printed on her Meritorious Service Medal citation for her 2022 to 2024 tour, signed by Brig. Gen. Amy S. Bumgarner: a team of 60 investigators from 17 agencies, “120 arrests and a 96 percent conviction rate.” It’s an Air Force record, and the citation is posted on her service page. [5]
She lies about founding an anti-child-predator program.
She never claimed to found ICAC. Her citation says she was one of the Air Force’s first agents trained for Internet Crimes Against Children cases. [5] She then helped stand up Hawaii’s ICAC task force, the team behind Operation Keiki Shield and Operation Shine the Light. [14][15] A task-force recognition plaque, Hawaii Attorney General releases and a letter from a retired Hawaii prosecutor back it up. [6]
An inspector-general report ties her to illegal policing.
It doesn’t. The report (DODIG-2016-075) reviewed the whole agency’s internet-crimes cases from 2010 to 2014. [16] It found the Air Force lacked a clear policy on agents’ roles in those task forces, and the agency issued a new one during the review. No agents are named in it or in the coverage of it. [17]
Her exit from active duty was “weird” and unexplained.
She left active duty in 2016 for the Air Force Reserve and kept serving until she retired on October 1, 2025. That’s a common career move. Both DD-214s, active duty and Reserve, are posted in full. [4]
She “reported for duty at Pete Hegseth’s Pentagon.”
Service members don’t pick their commanders. Her final assignment began in June 2024, and she retired on October 1, 2025. [4] By that logic, everyone who served in 2025 is a Hegseth loyalist, including the many Democrats in uniform.
She’s just a life coach whose service ended a decade ago.
She served until October 2025. [4] Her coaching practice, Mighty Sparrow Coaching, is a certified, service-disabled veteran-owned small business that trains federal, state, local and military teams on leadership, resilience, suicide prevention, and the work she did for 21 years: investigations, human trafficking and crimes against children. [18][19]
Her money-mindset coaching is a grift.
The Joyful Money Club is a small membership for women who already earn well and undervalue themselves. It teaches self-belief and an abundance mindset, and it tells people not to join unless they’re ready to do the work. [20] It’s coaching, not a get-rich-quick scheme.
There’s no way she’s been to 80 countries.
She grew up an Army and embassy kid, including years in Colombia while her father served at the U.S. embassy. [21] Her service record shows assignments and deployments across at least three continents. [4][11] As security advisor to the Secretary of the Air Force, a Secretary who visited more than 40 partner nations, she traveled with her across the UK, Japan, the Pacific, Israel and Europe. [11][22] Later she led investigations and law-enforcement development across Latin America for International Justice Mission. [11]
Her International Justice Mission title is made up.
From September 2016 to November 2017 she was International Justice Mission’s International Director of Investigations and Law Enforcement Development for Latin America, working on child sexual abuse and child sex trafficking cases. [11] The tax filings people point to list only the organization’s top officers and highest-paid staff, so they can’t show regional directors at all. [23] Her full civilian history is on alaniformt.com/service.
Why did she leave International Justice Mission after a year?
Her husband was reassigned to Hawaii. She went with him and took her investigative work to the Hawaii Attorney General’s office, where she helped build the state’s Internet Crimes Against Children task force. [11][14]
Her arrest numbers keep changing.
They’re different operations over different stretches of time, and each one is documented. Hawaii’s Operation Keiki Shield made 25 arrests in its first three rounds. [14] A 2021 Maui operation arrested six. [24] Her 2022 to 2024 Meritorious Service Medal citation lists 120 arrests and a 96 percent conviction rate. [5]
There’s no record of her as a Democrat before she ran.
Service members can’t do partisan politics in uniform. [25] For a federal agent, anything political you say publicly can be used to attack your testimony in court. Keeping her politics private for 21 years was part of the job.
Her treasurer ran the Pentagon’s cloud program, so she must be pro–data center.
Her treasurer is a retired Air Force officer the Air Force assigned to stand up its cloud program in 2018, after work at the White House under presidents of both parties. [26] That says where the Air Force sent her, not what Alani believes. Alani’s fight is with unregulated AI data centers and the sweetheart deals that come with them. [27]
“What if there are Signal messages, travel records…”
Of course she talked with Defense Department officials. She was a Defense Department special agent. Listing every kind of record that would prove a theory, without producing a single one, isn’t evidence.
## Faith and reproductive freedom
Nobody is questioning her opponents’ religion, or the views of their church leaders. Attending a church doesn’t sign anyone up for every belief its leaders hold, and a person’s faith should never be used against them. Alani’s policies are clear, and she believes strongly in the separation of church and state.
She belonged to a “pro-MAGA mega church.”
She first went to McLean Bible Church as a teenager, attended a few times a year while stationed in Washington, D.C., and left D.C. in 2017, [28] before President Trump visited it in 2019 and years before Roe fell in 2022. [29][30] Going to a church doesn’t mean holding every view its leaders take: most American Catholics say abortion should be legal in all or most cases. [31] Her positions on reproductive freedom and LGBTQ+ rights are public. [32]
She’s secretly a right-wing conservative because she talks about loving Jesus.
She has never hidden her faith. She calls herself “a Christian at my core” and non-denominational. Her record is public too: asked whether Congress should codify Roe, she said, “I absolutely think we should,” [33] and she was endorsed by NOW PAC, which backs only candidates who support reproductive rights. [34]
She waffled on abortion.
In the same interview the critics quote, she said, “I support people having the right to have an abortion,” and that Congress should codify Roe. [33] Saying what she would choose for herself is a personal decision, not a policy position.
She’s still paid by a far-right publisher.
She paid a publishing house a one-time fee to produce her 2023 book, and her Senate financial disclosure lists $201 to $1,000 in royalties from her own book. [35][28] Another author’s book on the same publisher’s list doesn’t make its views hers.
She may have sat “in the same pews” as a Republican strategist.
There’s no evidence they ever attended at the same time, let alone met. McLean Bible Church draws more than 10,000 people a week across several campuses and services. [29]
Planned Parenthood’s PAC endorsed her opponent, so she can’t be pro-choice. And she refused their survey.
Her record is on camera: asked whether Congress should codify Roe, she said, “I absolutely think we should,” [33] and NOW PAC and the National Women’s Political Caucus endorsed her. [34][36] Planned Parenthood Action Fund had already decided to back her opponent before it ever talked to the campaign, and its board member’s calls before the August 10 deadline were about getting her out of the race. No survey was ever sent. [37][38] At a forum she said she’d answered it. The ones she had answered were Montanans for Choice Take Action’s and NOW PAC’s, which endorsed her. [34] Montanans for Choice endorses no federal candidates, and it publishes her answers in full: a yes on all 13 of its reproductive-freedom positions. Kurt Alme didn’t respond. [39] She also answered the ERA Coalition’s Equal Rights Amendment survey, and its Elect Equality guide lists her as a supporter. Bodnar never responded; the guide lists him as “unknown.” [40] The campaign has apologized for the mix-up.
## The money
Notice who’s pushing the dark-money line. Seth Bodnar’s own super PAC runs on a dark-money chain. [41][42] Alani takes zero corporate PAC money and backs the ballot measure to end dark money in Montana. [43][44]
She “accepted millions in dark money.”
A candidate can’t accept independent expenditures. By law they’re made without the candidate’s involvement, and she has no say over them. [45] A super PAC spent about $2.3 million for her in the primary and then left the state. [46][47] Her own campaign takes $0 in corporate PAC money. [43]
She never spoke out about the dark money spent in the primary.
She did, before the primary. On May 21 her campaign issued a press release saying dark money “should be illegal, regardless as to whether it comes from the left or the right,” that the campaign does “not take any dark money, AIPAC, or corporate PAC money,” and that it had “done everything in its legal power to disavow dark money.” [48] The next day she posted the release and told voters on Facebook, “We have no control over the Super PACs pouring dark money into this race,” and “If the print at the bottom of any ad doesn’t say, ‘Paid for by Friends of Alani Bankhead,’ it’s not from this campaign.” [49][50] On May 30 she wrote that she had “categorically denounced all dark money and all the ads.” [51] Who was behind the pro-Alani spending wasn’t public then. Montana Free Press was still calling it a “mystery PAC” in July. [47] Save and share this graphic
A billionaire’s dark money bought her the primary.
Montana Democrats chose her in an open primary, 43.6 percent to 33.0 percent. [52] The money behind the pro-Alani primary spending traces back to the same source now funding her independent opponent’s super PAC. [41][42][53]
She coordinated with the outside PACs.
Independent expenditures are uncoordinated by law, [45] and no one has produced a single message, meeting or date that says otherwise. There’s nothing to produce, because it didn’t happen.
Those texts came from a Republican-aligned PAC that itself spent about $900,000 “supporting” her in the last two weeks of the primary while spending against her independent opponent. [54][53] Republicans want the vote split. Her campaign takes $0 in corporate PAC money. [43]
Republicans recruited her to split the vote.
If anyone had recruited her, she’d have had their money. Her campaign raised $58,829 through June 30, a shoestring by Senate standards. [43] The Republican-aligned spending in the primary was done to her, not with her, and the Washington Post predicted it on July 30. [55]
## “Plant,” “spoiler” and “not a real Democrat”
The only Montanans who have voted in this race chose her. Calling her a plant, a spoiler or a fake Democrat doesn’t change a single vote cast in the primary. [52]
She’s not a real Democrat.
She’s the Democratic nominee, chosen by Montana Democrats in an open primary. [52] The party’s executive director and staff stood with her at an Aug. 11 press conference. [56]
She came out of nowhere. She’s unvetted.
Montana primary voters vetted her, [52] and her record isn’t self-reported: DD-214s, general-signed citations, a retired Hawaii prosecutor’s letter, Hawaii Attorney General releases. [4][5][6][14] Her coaching and investigative work was public years before the campaign, from 2020 podcast interviews to her 2023 book. [12][57] It’s all at alaniformt.com/service.
She’s a Democratic plant who will drop out for the independent.
She didn’t drop out. The withdrawal deadline passed with her on the ballot, and she’s running through November 3. [58]
She’s a spoiler with no path.
Montana voters decide who has a path. The only Montanans who have voted in this race so far, in the primary, chose her. [52] “I am in this race to win it, and I am staying through November 3.” [58]
She’s staying in the race just to help Republicans.
That quote is spliced together from her words and a reporter’s paraphrase. [55][37] Her actual reason: she won the primary, and a split vote is the independent’s problem to solve. See the splice on /truth.
She’ll work with Trump.
Her test is what’s good for Montana. She’s on record against the war in Iran (“I am completely opposed to this war”) and against the tariffs raising Montanans’ costs. [59] Every position is here.
She doesn’t have the experience to be a senator.
None of the four candidates for this seat has held elected office. What she has done is stand up teams and build coalitions: she directed more than 180 agents across eight countries, guarded the Secretary of the Air Force through 47 countries, and twice brought seventeen law enforcement agencies together against child predators, in Hawaii and on her final Air Force tour. [4][5] How all four candidates have led, side by side.
## The party chair’s op-ed
On Oct. 12 the Montana Democratic Party’s chair, Shannon O’Brien, resigned and endorsed the independent in an MS NOW opinion piece. [60] These are the claims it made about Alani, and the record on each. The campaign’s full response, with every source linked, is at alaniformt.com/pr-2026-10-12.
She refuses to listen and won’t take advice.
O’Brien wrote that Alani “has refused advice from experienced business and political leaders around the state.” [60] The piece doesn’t say what that advice was. The advice, on the public record and behind closed doors, was to quit. The only thing she refused was the demand to withdraw: a July 9 letter from 17 Democratic legislators urging one of the two candidates out, [61] an Aug. 7 letter from 22 naming her, [62] a former party chair’s open letter saying there was “not a viable path,” [63] and the national Senate committee telling Semafor she had no path to victory. [64] A leaked “How to Help” document urged people to contact her family. [65][66][67] She spoke at the Montana Democratic Party’s state convention, [68] stayed on the ballot through the withdrawal deadline, and kept campaigning with county Democrats across the state. “I am in this race to win it, and I am staying through November 3.” [58]
The party chair stayed neutral until she resigned.
On July 30 O’Brien convened the party’s executive board to discuss leaving the Democratic line empty. [69] Before the withdrawal deadline, she requested a legal opinion from the Elias Law Group on whether the party could be forced to name a replacement if Alani withdrew. Board members had not voted to seek it. “This was Shannon getting legal analysis,” the party’s own spokesperson said. She shared the “private and confidential” document with county party leaders, and some board members suggested reviewing her performance as chair. [70] Days later the party’s executive director stood with Alani and said, “What happened to Alani Bankhead, myself, my staff, our executive board was unacceptable.” [56]
Republicans wanted her on the ballot.
More Jobs, Less Government, a super PAC aligned with Sen. Steve Daines, spent $901,179 “supporting” her in the last two weeks of the primary while spending $962,124 against the independent. The same PAC spent $12.9 million against Jon Tester in 2024. [54] She never asked for any of it, and her campaign’s May 21 release called on Kurt Alme to tell Sen. Daines to “stop the dark money influx via More Jobs, Less Government and any other PAC.” [48] More on the Republican spending.
There are real questions about her commitment to abortion rights.
She’s pro-choice. She supports the Women’s Health Protection Act and a constitutional amendment protecting abortion rights, and she opposes any federal abortion ban. [32] NOW PAC and the National Women’s Political Caucus endorsed her, [34][36] and she answered yes to all 13 of Montanans for Choice’s questions. [39] She also answered the ERA Coalition’s Equal Rights Amendment survey, and its Elect Equality guide lists her as a supporter. Bodnar never responded; the guide lists him as “unknown.” [40] More in Faith & choice.
Her views on people in poverty.
The line comes from a December 2025 money-mindset coaching episode that opens with clients who earned over $300,000 a year and were still broke. [71] The full answer is here, and her plan for working families is at alaniformt.com/positions.
She’s almost brand new to Montana.
She grew up an Army and embassy kid, then served 21 years in the Air Force. Every home before Montana was chosen by the military. Montana is the first place she chose. She has lived in Montana almost five years. More here.
She has no momentum or resources.
Through Aug. 31, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee had sent $0 to the Montana Democratic Party this cycle, compared with $2.8 million over the same stretch in 2024. [72] The national party starved its own nominee, then cited the starvation.
She came out of the gate mudslinging at the independent for no reason.
The reason was public. Two weeks after winning the primary, she asked him to leave the race. She pointed to the gender-discrimination lawsuit from his time as University of Montana president, which settled for $350,000, and argued the Democratic Party has to have a candidate on the ballot, so he should be the one to step aside. [73] It’s the same argument party insiders then spent four months making to her.
Read the campaign’s full Oct. 12 response to Shannon O’Brien, with every source: alaniformt.com/pr-2026-10-12.
## The Billings canvass
A letter in the Billings Gazette on Oct. 18 said the campaign “exploits working people” and didn’t pay the people who knocked doors in Billings. The campaign hired a vendor, Sole Strategies, to run that canvass, and paid it in full before the first door. The campaign’s full statement, with the contract language, is at alaniformt.com/pr-2026-10-18.
The canvassers worked for the campaign.
They worked for Sole Strategies. The contract states: “All canvassers and internal Sole Strategies staff are not employees of the campaign, they are contractors employed by Sole Strategies.”
The campaign didn’t pay the people who knocked doors.
The campaign paid Sole the full amount on Sept. 1, two weeks before the first door was ever knocked. That amount covers “Canvasser pay… Payroll and HR” per the signed contract. Paying the crew was Sole’s job.
The campaign knows what the canvassers were paid and is hiding it.
The campaign has never seen those numbers. The contract states Sole “is happy to provide timesheets upon request.” The campaign asked for them in writing twice, and Sole refused. If anyone who knocked doors in Billings wasn’t paid in full by Sole, the campaign has asked them to reach out directly at press@alanibankheadforsenate.com so the campaign can work to make it right for them, even if Sole Strategies has not.
Read the campaign’s full Oct. 18 statement: alaniformt.com/pr-2026-10-18.
## Everything else
Every one of these started the same way: a clip, a screenshot or a secondhand post, passed along until it sounded like a fact. None of them came with a document. Alani’s record does.
She worked with ICE agents and called them “amazing people.”
She was talking about Homeland Security Investigations, the federal unit that works online child-exploitation cases. It was one of more than a dozen agencies on Operation Keiki Shield, catching people trying to meet children for sex. [14] Praising the agents who caught child predators has nothing to do with immigration raids. Her immigration plan is here.
She loves the IDF and Mossad, so she sympathizes with crimes in Gaza.
As a federal agent she worked with foreign partner agencies; that’s the job. Her position: stop underwriting the suffering in Gaza, condition and block arms transfers, and enforce the Leahy Law. [74]
She said poor people chose to be poor.
It’s from a December 2025 coaching episode about a client household earning $300,000 a year that was still broke. [71] Her point was about mindset with money, and it wasn’t about Montanans struggling to get by. Her plan for working families is on her positions page. [28] Another clip they use stops mid-thought. The next sentence: “But it’s how you respond to those things that indicates the quality of your life.”
She’s only lived in Montana three years.
She grew up an Army and embassy kid, then served 21 years in the Air Force. [21][4] Every home before Montana was picked by the military. Montana is the first place she chose. She has lived in Montana almost five years.
She has a “secret” Facebook account.
It’s a privacy alias. After years of undercover work against child predators, she kept her real name off social media. [75] Seth’s campaign has now published the alias on its website.
She promoted an antisemitic rapper (the Yeezy shirt).
It was a joke T-shirt from 2016, years before Ye’s antisemitic rants. Her husband wore a “Deez Nuts” shirt the same day.
She associates with a January 6th rioter (Sam Redfern).
Alani doesn’t condone Sam Redfern’s past behavior. She does respect anyone doing that work. He’s an active supporter of I-194, the ballot measure to end dark money, and he has met with leaders across the spectrum, including former Gov. Brian Schweitzer and former congressional candidate Russell Cleveland, who posted their photo together from an I-194 event in Whitefish on October 7 (photo). Seth Bodnar is the last person who should complain about meeting across the aisle. On October 13 he invited President Trump to sit down with him: “I will come to meet you whenever and wherever your schedule allows.” (his letter)
She has “a pattern of associating with violent extremists and antisemites.”
That’s the headline on a page Seth Bodnar’s campaign built about her (archived copy). Its evidence is the T-shirt and the interview above.
Her family is fair game.
Seth’s campaign website now names and links to members of Alani’s family. If he thinks families are fair game, we disagree completely, and we condemn it.
She laughed when Kyle Austin called Native Americans “pets.”
She didn’t laugh at it. The smile in Seth Bodnar’s clip comes seconds after the remark, from a side conversation that carried over from before the forum. She condemned it: Austin’s comment, she said, “was wrong and reflected a serious misunderstanding of tribal sovereignty and the federal government’s relationship with tribal nations.” Seth spoke right after Austin, asked for the question to be repeated, and said nothing about it at the forum. Watch the full forum from Austin’s answer, and read the full answer on /truth.
## The record they can’t argue with
- 21 years in the U.S. Air Force. Retired as a lieutenant colonel on October 1, 2025.
- Special agent, Air Force Office of Special Investigations.
- Arrested child predators, hunted traffickers, and ran counterintelligence operations on multiple continents.
- Served in Iraq (Iraq Campaign Medal) and commanded in the Gulf.
- Security advisor to the Secretary of the Air Force.
- Both DD-214s, her decoration citations and letters, posted in full.

## Senate rejects health care plans as ACA tax credits near expiration
The Senate blocked an extension of ACA tax credits, set to expire Jan. 1, potentially raising premiums for millions of Americans.
Scripps News Group. Dec 11, 2025
